newsitem.title: USA: Discount chain Target stops selling cigarettes.
newsitem.headline: Discount chain Target stops selling cigarettes.

text.p: Discount store giant Target, citing rising costs of carrying tabacco products, said Wednesday it will stop selling cigarettes, but few other retailers were poised to follow its lead.
Target, the nation's third-largest discount store chain, said the expense of complying with local restrictions on cigarette sales and declining profits prompted the decision.
The retailer plans to remove cigarettes from its shelves by the end of September.
"It's really a business decision," said Susan Eich, a spokeswoman for Target, a unit of Dayton Hudson Corp..
"Obviously a lot of people are going to be happy or unhappy about this, regardless of the rationale," she said.

More than a dozen states have sued the tobacco industry in recent weeks. In Michigan, which took aim not only at cigarette producers but also at their wholesale distributors, a lawsuit brought last week named Wal-Mart Stores Inc.'s Sam's wholesale warehouse club as a defendant.
Target said its decision was not a response to the recent wave of lawsuits. Rather, the company said the costs of staying in the business outweighed the benefits.

Demands that local governments and cigarette producers have placed on retailers to stem sales to minors have made it more costly to sell tobacco products, analysts said. Still, most chains ring up fat profits on the merchandise.
"If Target doesn't sell them, someone else will," said Ronald Morrow of Rodman & Renshaw Inc.

Several of Target's competitors, including Wal-Mart Stores Inc., the nation's largest retailer, and Kmart Corp., said they plan to continue carrying cigarettes. Industry trade groups said Target was the only national retailer that they were aware of to pull the products from its stores recently.
"It's a profitable part of our business, and we'll continue to sell them responsibly," said Kmart spokeswoman Teresa Fearon.
Short of a joint effort by America's retailers to stop selling cigarettes, tabacco producers will not feel much of a pinch.
"The best chance to reduce consumption in the United States is congressional legislation," said Martin Feldman of Smith Barney.
Cigarettes make up less than a half of 1 percentage point of Target's annual sales, and sales volume at its stores have slipped in recent years, company spokeswoman Eich said.
Drugstore retailer Walgreen Co. said cigarettes, chewing tobacco and other tobacco goods make up about 4 percent of yearly sales, and it has no immediate plans to stop selling them.
"We don't anticipate any change, but we will continue reviewing it like we do with any other product category," a spokesman for the Deerfield, Ill.-based retailer said.
Stores that Target has opened during the last year, or about 20 percent of the chain, do not carry cigarettes.
The steep cost of building special counters to control tabacco sales, along with a high theft rate, made it expensive to sell cigarettes.
Snack foods and sports trading cards will be stocked where cigarettes once were displayed.
Target said it informed distributors of its decision last month. Philip Morris Cos Inc. is the retailer's largest supplier of cigarettes.
